report:
**Conclusion:** Your sister’s claim is supported by the best direct randomized evidence, but the benefit is modest rather than certain in every setting.

The pivotal multicenter randomized trial compared chlorhexidine–alcohol with iodine–alcohol before cesarean delivery. Surgical-site infection within 30 days occurred in **4.0%** (23 patients) with chlorhexidine–alcohol versus **7.3%** (42) with iodine–alcohol—an absolute reduction of **3.3 percentage points** (roughly 1 fewer infection per 30 preparations), relative risk **0.55** (95% CI 0.34–0.90; *P*=0.02). This is strong, directly applicable evidence for the precise comparison in the claim.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1511048

The broader evidence is directionally consistent but less definitive. A Cochrane review judged the evidence **moderate certainty** and concluded chlorhexidine gluconate probably *slightly* reduces SSI compared with povidone-iodine. “Iodine” preparations and application methods varied across included studies, so it does not mean chlorhexidine will outperform every iodine-based protocol in every hospital.  
https://www.cochrane.org/CD007462/PREG_skin-preparation-preventing-infection-following-caesarean-section

Some smaller trials did not individually find a statistically significant difference, likely partly because they lacked power; for example, one pilot RCT reported a lower but nonsignificant risk with chlorhexidine–alcohol.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34404473/

WHO’s 2021 cesarean-specific guidance supersedes its earlier advice on this question, reflecting the evolving evidence base. In practice, clinician choice must also consider chlorhexidine allergy, safe drying of alcohol-containing solutions (fire risk), and local protocols.  
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK571507/
